must_understand: two different questions: whether app customers are worth more (a question about customers and their value) and a demand forecast by category and emirate
value has to be measured per customer, not per order or per channel total, and the same customer can buy through several channels, so customers cannot simply be labelled by channel
even if app customers spend more, that does not show that moving ad money to the app would bring more value: they may be the keen customers who would buy anyway

orders that were refunded or cancelled, repeated rows and missing amounts must be handled before any revenue figure, and a forecast for each category and emirate from about fifteen months of orders needs a range
acceptable_approaches: define revenue first (status, repeated rows, missing amounts), then compare spend per customer by the channels each customer uses, said to be a description
suggest a test (a share of the budget moved for a period or a region) to learn what the app spend actually brings
a simple seasonal forecast per category and emirate, with a range and its limits, pooling small emirates when their numbers are thin
forbidden: tells the COO that moving the budget to the app will raise revenue, from channel averages
compares channels by order totals without looking at customers who buy through more than one channel
gives single forecast numbers with no range

must_understand: the outcome is leaving next month, and the prediction is made at the start of the month, before any of that month's events
the person thinks the ticket count may run up to the day of cancelling: that must be checked, because tickets raised while cancelling would give the answer away
a list of who is at risk is not the same as knowing who an offer will keep: a call can only be judged by a test with a group not called
the team can only call so many customers, so the model should be judged on the customers it puts at the top of the list, not on accuracy
acceptable_approaches: ask or check when the ticket window ends, and leave the column out or rebuild it to stop before the prediction moment if it is unclear
a classification model with a holdout that respects time, judged on the share of leavers caught in the top of the list the team can call
propose a small test with a random group not called to measure what the offer keeps
forbidden: uses the ticket count as an input without checking when it is counted
judges the model by accuracy alone
claims the calls will keep a given number of customers, from the model's scores alone

must_understand: two steps in order: cleaning the bookings so they can be added up, then a monthly report built on the clean table
the price is stored as text with the currency in it and has to become a number, and some rows are test bookings that must not count
the person's claim that the export is ready to use is wrong and must be checked, not trusted
the report must say which date it groups by (booking date or travel date), because cancelled revenue by month changes with that choice
acceptable_approaches: profile the table first and list each fix with how many rows it touches (price text, test rows, repeated bookings)
state the definition of cancelled revenue and the month it is grouped by, then build the monthly table by destination
keep the cleaning as steps that can be rerun on the next export
forbidden: adds up the price column as it is, or drops prices it cannot read without saying so
keeps the test bookings in the report
builds a model when the person asked for clean data and a report

must_understand: the unit is a pipe (or a stretch of main) and the outcome is a burst within a set period, such as the next year, judged before that period starts

the person's test of success is flawed: a replaced pipe is new, so its bursts fall whatever the model did; success has to be judged against pipes not replaced, or against the model's ranking on years it did not see
the burst records may only include pipes still in the register: pipes already replaced or removed are missing, which can bias the history
the budget fixes how many pipes can be chosen, so the model is judged on how many bursts its top two percent would have caught
acceptable_approaches: a burst-risk model per pipe with a holdout of later years, judged on bursts caught in the top two percent
a simple baseline first (age and material, and past bursts on the same pipe) to compare against
a way to judge the programme: compare the ranked pipes with similar pipes not replaced, or keep part of the choice outside the model
forbidden: accepts that falling bursts on replaced pipes prove the model works
uses a random split of pipe-years so later bursts help predict earlier ones
promises a number of bursts avoided before any data has been seen

must_understand: a good placement has to be defined, for example still in the job after three months, and it is only known for people who were interviewed and placed
past decisions chose who got a label: a model trained only on placed people learns the recruiters' old choices, and says nothing reliable about the people never interviewed

using the score to decide who gets an interview affects people's access to work, so personal traits such as age, sex or origin, and fields that stand in for them, need care and checking for unfair differences
the score should be judged at the moment of application, on later applicants than it was trained on, and on the forty the recruiters can see
acceptable_approaches: define the outcome and the moment of prediction, and say which applicants have a known outcome
a model with a time-ordered holdout, a check of how its ranking differs across groups of applicants, and a human still making the interview choice
suggest interviewing a small random share outside the ranking to learn about the people the old process never saw
forbidden: treats applicants who were never interviewed as bad placements
builds the ranking without any check for unfair differences between groups
lets the score decide alone who gets an interview, with no person in the loop

must_understand: two parts: a dashboard of churn by city over time, and a grouping of customers for marketing
the table is one snapshot with a single churn flag for next month, so it cannot show how churn moved month by month; that needs a history of monthly snapshots
monthly spend has missing values, and business and consumer customers behave differently, which both matter for the grouping
groups made for marketing are a description and need to be checked to be stable and useful, not taken as true types of customer
acceptable_approaches: say what the dashboard can show from this table (churn rate by city and plan now, with its uncertainty) and what history is needed for a trend
a simple grouping from tenure, plan, spend and segment, handled for missing spend, with each group described in plain words
propose saving a monthly snapshot from now on so the trend can be built
forbidden: draws a churn trend over time from the single snapshot, for example by signup month as if it were churn month
fills missing spend with zero without saying so
presents the groups as a model of who will churn

must_understand: two parts: forecasting demand per sailing, and choosing a fare from it; the second needs to know how demand reacts to price
fares were raised by hand on the sailings expected to be busy, so in the history high fares go with high demand: the history cannot show how people react to price on its own
the demand forecast has to be made at the moment the fare is set, before the booking curve is known, and judged on later sailings
capacity caps what was booked, so a full sailing hides how many more wanted to travel
acceptable_approaches: a demand forecast per sailing from what is known at fare-setting time, with a holdout of later sailings
measure price response with small planned fare changes on comparable sailings, rather than from the hand-set history
treat full sailings as at least that much demand, not exactly that much
forbidden: reads from the history that higher fares bring more passengers, or fits price response from it without saying it is confounded
sets automatic fares from the model with no test or limit
treats bookings on full sailings as the true demand

must_understand: two parts: checking the claim about how late British customers book, and forecasting trips by travel month
the claim has to be checked in the data, with the spread of lead times, not just an average; in this table British lead times are close to everyone else's
the latest travel months are still filling up: bookings for them keep arriving, so their counts are incomplete and cannot be read as falling demand
test bookings and cancelled bookings have to be handled before counting trips
acceptable_approaches: compare lead times by nationality with their spread and the number of bookings, and say plainly whether the claim holds
forecast travel months from how far each month had filled at the same lead time in the past, with a range
state whether cancelled bookings count as sold trips, and drop the test rows
forbidden: agrees that British customers book much later without checking
reads the low counts of the latest travel months as a fall in demand
gives a single forecast number per month with no range
